Living bodies count as reservoirs too, since they store carbon, water, and nitrogen.
questions.misconception: Processes such as photosynthesis are places, or reservoirs such as soil are only pathways that matter passes through without stopping.
questions.hint: Ask: is this a place where atoms can sit, or something that happens to carry atoms somewhere?

questions.explanation: Matter cycles. Atoms of water, carbon, and nitrogen pass from the air, water, and soil into living things and back again, joining different molecules along the way. Nothing is used up: the same atoms keep being reused, while energy from the Sun flows through and leaves as heat.
questions.misconception: Living things use up matter, or matter turns into energy.
questions.hint: Think about where the atoms in a fallen leaf go after it drops.

evidence.supports: The same matter moves continuously in a global cycle throughout Earth's ecosystems, taking on different forms as it moves.
Matter cycles continuously among living and nonliving parts of Earth's ecosystems; it is never lost but changes form.

questions.prompt: Two newly planted forests are the same size. Forest 1 is in a warm, rainy place with a ten-month growing season. Forest 2 is in a cold, dry place with a three-month growing season. Which forest will most likely capture carbon faster, and why?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Two newly planted forests are the same size. Forest 1 is in a warm, rainy place with a ten-month growing season. Forest 2 is in a cold, dry place with a three-month growing season. Which forest will most likely capture carbon faster, and why?
questions.conditions: Both forests have the same number of young trees, and nothing such as fire or logging disturbs either one.
questions.limitations: Real forest growth also depends on soil, tree species, and other factors; this comparison looks only at warmth, water, and season length.

choices.text: Forest 2, since cold air holds more carbon dioxide for the trees to use.
choices.rationale: Trees take carbon dioxide from the air in both places. How fast they capture it depends on how fast they photosynthesize, and cold, dry weather slows that down.

choices.text: Forest 1, since its warm weather lets the trees pull carbon from the soil.
choices.rationale: Forest 1 is the better choice, but not for this reason. Trees build wood from carbon dioxide in the air, not from carbon in the soil.

choices.text: Forest 1, since more water and a longer season mean more photosynthesis.
choices.rationale: Correct. Trees grow fastest with plenty of water and a long growing season. More growth means more photosynthesis, which pulls carbon dioxide out of the air faster.

choices.text: Both the same, since two forests of equal size capture carbon at the same rate.
choices.rationale: Equal size does not mean equal growth. Forest 1's trees have more water and more than three times as many growing months, so they photosynthesize far more each year.

questions.explanation: Trees capture carbon through photosynthesis, so whatever speeds up their growth speeds up capture. Plenty of water, warmth, and a long growing season let Forest 1's trees photosynthesize for more of the year. That is why engineers planning reforestation look for sunny, well-watered sites where the growing season lasts many months.
questions.misconception: Cold air holds more carbon dioxide for trees, forests of the same size capture carbon at the same rate, or trees get their carbon from the soil.
questions.hint: What does a tree need to grow quickly, and which forest gives it more of those things?

evidence.supports: Trees grow especially fast where light and water are plentiful and growing seasons are long, and the faster they grow, the faster they photosynthesize and remove carbon dioxide from the air.
When trees carry out photosynthesis, they capture carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and store the carbon in their body structures as biomass.
